meta.title: Organizational Behavior
meta.one_liner: Motivation, teams, decisions, negotiation, leadership, and change, taught through Harvard cases and simulations.
meta.blurb: This was the core organizational behavior course for business students at CMU Qatar, and the course I taught most during my years in Doha. I built it around cases and simulations: Lincoln Electric and SAS for motivation, an Everest simulation and the Carter Racing exercise for team decisions, live negotiations, and a change simulation at the end. Each year I replaced more lecture time with exercises, so students spent most of class applying a concept rather than hearing about it. Students finished by analyzing a real company of their choosing with the course's frameworks.
meta.scale: About 70 to 90 students a year across two sections

assignments.name: Exams
assignments.description: Two non-cumulative, closed-book exams mixing multiple choice, short answer, and essay questions.

assignments.name: Quizzes
assignments.description: Seven open-book online quizzes on the previous one to two weeks of lectures, readings, and cases.

assignments.name: Group case analysis papers
assignments.description: Four papers written in randomly assigned groups. Assignment 1 analyzed the SAS Institute case. Assignment 2 analyzed the team's own Everest simulation run alongside the 1996 Everest case. Assignment 3 had groups carry out two negotiations outside class, a movie production deal and a hotel coffee contract, and report their planning, BATNAs, and outcomes. Assignment 4 compared Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, and a leader of the group's choice using Kotter, Goleman's six styles, and StrengthsFinder.

assignments.name: Final project
assignments.description: In self-selected groups of three to five, students analyzed a real organization using three course topics, backed by at least six sources, and recommended improvements. Each group wrote an 8 to 10 page paper and gave a five-minute presentation. Companies from earlier course cases or earlier years were off limits.

assignments.name: Classroom engagement
assignments.description: Discussion, in-class exercises, and iClicker questions, with some cold calling so quieter students had an equal chance to contribute. Peer evaluations after every group assignment fed into this grade.
